The Evidence Ladder

Opinion, intent, behaviour, payment — and why the rung is a property of the pair (assumption, test), not of the test.

1. Opening: two rooms, seventeen days apart

On Tuesday 22 September 2026, Jeevika Lakdawala, vice-president of product at Quila Diagnostics in Bengaluru, sat with a slide she had asked for twice and liked neither time. Quila collected blood samples at home and returned reports in its app; 2,18,000 households had bought at least one test. The proposal was QoVitals, a quarterly subscription at ₹1,499 bundling a full panel with a physician-reviewed trend report. Her research lead, Jharna Lavania, had run a fake door on it for a quarter. Her chief financial officer, Jehangir Lakhera, priced it at ₹14.60 lakh of fixed cost a quarter — two part-time reviewing physicians at ₹5.20 lakh each, a ₹3.00 lakh minimum on a dedicated laboratory contract, ₹1.20 lakh of platform and operations — plus ₹410 a subscriber-quarter for phlebotomy and reagents.

The funnel ended with 171 households who had paid ₹1,499 twice: the top rung by any reading. Break-even was 1,341 subscribers. Lakdawala's problem was not weak evidence but strong evidence that said no, in a room explaining why the sample had been unfair to the idea.

Seventeen days later, on Friday 9 October 2026, Jaiveer Lahane faced the mirror image in Pune. Lahane ran product at Quorum Freight Cloud, a transport management system with 340 mid-market manufacturing accounts, and had closed a three-month paid pilot of QoDock, a dock-appointment scheduling module at ₹18,000 per plant per month. Ten accounts paid; 200 named users were provisioned; 90 activated; six accounts renewed at month four. His sales lead, Jasmit Ladkat, wanted to multiply 45 per cent activation by the install base and book the number. His staff data scientist, Jugal Longkumer, had sent one line the night before: that is not 200 observations, it is ten.

Lahane's evidence was also top-rung and, for his decision, close to worthless. Both rooms had climbed the ladder correctly and both were about to make an error it does not warn against. The ladder is a good first-order instrument and a poor final one: what it proxies can be computed exactly, and experts spend their effort on the conditions it omits.

2. The idea: a signalling model in a staircase costume

The evidence ladder ranks proof about a customer assumption by what it cost the customer to produce: opinion (free), stated intent (free, and flattering), free behaviour (seconds), costly commitment (a deposit, a signature, an hour, data access) and paid usage, with repeated payment at the top. Match the rung to the cost of being wrong.

Three lineages converge on it. The economic one runs from Paul Samuelson's revealed-preference work of 1938 and 1948, which made choice under constraint rather than report the observable primitive of demand, through four decades of argument about hypothetical bias in contingent valuation — the 1993 NOAA panel against Diamond and Hausman in 1994 — and Juster's 1966 purchase-probability scale, that tradition's constructive reply: intent is biased but calibratable if you keep records. The product-development lineage supplies the practice: Blank's customer development, Ries's build-measure-learn, Fitzpatrick's argument in The Mom Test (2013) that only commitment and advancement inform, and Bland and Osterwalder's Testing Business Ideas (2019), the first widely used text to rank evidence strength beside each experiment type.

The third lineage, signalling, supplies the correction experts actually carry. Spence's 1973 model and Zahavi's 1975 handicap principle make precise what the ladder says loosely: a signal separates good types from bad not because it is costly but because it is differentially costly — cheaper for the type you want. Ladder height proxies differential cost, and the proxy breaks wherever the signal's price is refunded, reimbursed, subsidised, or paid by someone other than the person whose behaviour you are forecasting.

3. Mechanics in depth: the rung is a likelihood ratio

Expert practice replaces "how high is this evidence?" with "how far should this result move my belief?" Where a team keeps records that has an exact answer: a likelihood ratio. For a pass/fail test the positive likelihood ratio is the probability of passing when the assumption is true over the probability of passing when it is false, and posterior odds equal prior odds times that ratio. Between 2022 and 2026 Quorum tested 34 assumptions twice — once with a fake door, once with a paid pilot — shipped all 34, and recorded whether each met a bar written down beforehand. Ten met it.

The ladder had the ordering right; it cannot give the size of the gap, and the size decides whether a test earns its cost.

The step always left implicit: what is the information worth?

Lahane must decide whether to roll QoDock out to the full install base. Rollout costs ₹1.45 crore in year one. Lahane brackets first-year revenue at ₹2.20 crore if renewal across the base settles near 30 per cent and ₹1.10 crore if near 15 per cent — stipulated brackets, not measured rates. The pilot's own 60 per cent, which would imply ₹4.41 crore, is excluded because those ten accounts volunteered and no rung cures that selection. Call the brackets high and low, prior 40 per cent on high; payoffs +₹0.75 crore and −₹0.35 crore. Building is worth 0.40 × 0.75 + 0.60 × (−0.35) = ₹0.09 crore against zero for not building, so Quorum should build, barely. With perfect foreknowledge it would build only in the high state, worth 0.40 × 0.75 = ₹0.30 crore, so perfect information is worth 0.30 − 0.09 = ₹0.21 crore. That ₹21 lakh is a hard ceiling on what any test on this decision can be worth, at any rung, with any sample size.

A rung-5 test on randomly selected accounts carries LR+ 6.40 and LR− 0.229. Prior odds 0.667, so a pass gives odds 4.267, or 81.0 per cent, and a failure 0.152, or 13.2 per cent; the chance of a pass is 0.80 × 0.40 + 0.125 × 0.60 = 0.395. On a pass, building is worth 0.810 × 0.75 + 0.190 × (−0.35) = +₹0.541 crore, so Quorum builds; on a failure, 0.132 × 0.75 + 0.868 × (−0.35) = −₹0.205 crore, so it banks zero. The decision is worth 0.395 × 0.541 = ₹0.214 crore with the test and ₹0.09 crore without: ₹12.38 lakh of gain, inside the ₹21 lakh ceiling, against ₹11 lakh of cost.

The rung-3 test is sharper still. A pass moves the probability to 40.7 per cent and a failure to 34.8 per cent; building is worth +₹0.097 crore at the first and +₹0.033 crore at the second. Both are positive. Whatever the fake door says, Quorum builds — so the test's value is exactly zero. The ledger agrees: 0.885 × 0.097 + 0.115 × 0.033 = ₹0.090 crore, identical to the no-test figure. It is not weak evidence; it is not evidence, because no outcome it can produce changes an action. 4. When the ladder applies, and when it actively misleads

Four conditions, stated as testable claims. One: the payer is the actor. True for Lakdawala, where the household pays and is tested; false for Lahane, where central IT paid and dock supervisors act. Two: the sacrifice is not refunded, reimbursed or credited. True of Quila's ₹1,499; false of its ₹299 hold and of QoFleet's deposits. Three: the test's action resembles the shipped one closely enough that passing one predicts passing the other. Partly true for Quila, whose manual pilot delivered a slower report than the product would; false for Lahane, whose module Quorum's staff configured. Four: the units are independent, or the dependence is modelled. True for Quila's 46,300 households; decisively false for Lahane's 200 seats inside ten accounts. A fifth, usually unstated: the evidence and the threshold must be the same kind of quantity — a cohort's survivors are not a steady-state stock.

Where all four hold the ladder is close to sufficient. Where condition one or two fails it is actively misleading, ranking a worthless test above a useful one and handing the team the confidence of the top rung. The dangerous case is not a team on rung two that knows it; it is one that has been issued a receipt.

5. Hard edge cases

Two-sided markets. The ladder is climbed twice, and a result on one side is no result, because each side's willingness is conditional on the other's: a seller's letter of intent signed when demand is promised has near-zero differential cost. Mature marketplaces sequence non-refundable commitments instead — sellers list real inventory at real prices before buyers see anything, and the listing's opportunity cost is the measurement.

Regulated products. In lending, insurance and diagnostics the top rung is sometimes illegal to reach; Quila cannot sell a panel it has not validated. The answer is a legal costly signal — a completed KYC submission, a bureau-pull consent, a prescription uploaded — each costing real effort and privacy, and predicting better than intent.

Hardware plus software. Pre-orders are the classic top-rung instrument and the classic trap: one taken at a launch discount measures price sensitivity at the discount, and the deposit is refundable until shipment. Firms that do it well run two cohorts — refundable at the discount, non-refundable at list — and forecast from the latter.

AI-native products. Users will pay for a demonstration that works on their chosen example and abandon a product that works, say, 83 in 100 times on their real workload, so payment proves willingness to pay for the promise, not the realised quality distribution. The construct needing a test is tolerance for a given error rate on a given task, and the test that reaches it is a paid run on the customer's backlog with failures visible and uncorrected.

6. Four nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

A rung belongs to a pair, not to a test

The competent practitioner says "we ran a paid pilot, so we have rung-5 evidence." The expert asks: for which assumption? Lahane's pilot is rung 5 for will a budget holder approve ₹18,000 a month and rung 3 for will dock supervisors use the scheduler. The tell is a deck that prints the test and its rung in a header rather than each assumption with its own rung.

The denominator is where the lying happens

Lavania's first draft reported the click rate as 3,241 of 2,18,000 registered households, or 1.49 per cent, and read as a disaster. But the door lived on the post-report screen, and only 46,300 households opened a report in the window. The right rate is 3,241 of 46,300, or 7.00 per cent. Name the eligible population aloud before computing any ratio, over the same period as the numerator.

Strong evidence about a narrow group does not license a narrow launch

Quila's renewals were concentrated: 121 of the 171 came from the 7,900 households with three or more prior tests, 1.53 per cent against 0.13 per cent elsewhere. The reflex is to serve the dense segment only, and it is wrong whenever the cost covered is fixed, because narrowing cuts the numerator and leaves the denominator alone. Section 8 shows broad clearing break-even and narrow failing it on identical evidence. The companion working-knowledge page on this topic reaches the opposite verdict, and correctly: there, narrowing removed a tutor's salary, cutting fixed cost as well as revenue. The question is never whether the segment is denser but whether narrowing removes the cost.

Clustered units inflate confidence beyond any rung's power to repair

Ninety activations out of 200 seats is 45 per cent, and 200 is a comfortable number. But the seats sit in ten accounts and behaviour inside an account is correlated: a plant that trains its supervisors has many activations, one that does not has few. Count independent decisions — here ten. The arithmetic below widens the 95 per cent interval from 38–52 to 29–61 per cent, bringing a 35 per cent threshold inside it.

7. How it differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products the rupee is cheap to collect and the discipline problem is stopping short at the taps. In B2B and enterprise the rupee is slow and payer and user diverge, which is where the pair-not-test nuance does most of its work; the substitute currencies are a named internal owner with a diary commitment, a completed security review and production data handed over, each costing political capital. In platforms and marketplaces the ladder is climbed twice. In hardware the top rung is reachable but contaminated by refundability and launch pricing. In AI products payment proves appetite for the promise, little about tolerance for error.

Across stages the difference is smaller than claimed. An early-stage team has no record from which to compute a likelihood ratio, so it uses the ladder as a heuristic and accepts the error; it also has so little capital that nearly every cheap test is worth running, which makes the value-of-information calculation moot. A scaled company can compute likelihood ratios — Quorum's 34-row record took four years and is the most valuable artefact in its product function — but faces a political economy in which low-rung evidence is attractive because it cannot refuse a plan. What does not change with stage is the arithmetic of bases, clustering, stocks and differential cost.

Three: QoFleet, where the top rung failed, and the recovery

In March 2025 Quorum collected letters of intent from 14 transport contractors for QoFleet, an electronic proof-of-delivery app, each with a ₹25,000 deposit — ₹3.50 lakh, signed and banked. Quorum built it over three quarters at ₹1.42 crore and launched in January 2026. Twelve of the 14 deployed, provisioning 2,940 drivers, and in month two 318 of them used the app: 10.8 per cent.

Two failures of condition, not of arithmetic. The deposit was credited in full against the first year's licence fee, so its differential cost to an uninterested contractor was zero: a discount voucher with a signature attached. And the payer was the owner while the actor was the driver — capture took roughly 2.5 minutes per delivery against about 20 seconds for the paper pod it replaced. The test was rung five for will owners sign and rung zero for will drivers use, and nobody had written the second assumption down.

The recovery priced the sacrifice in the currency drivers spend, which is time. Two field staff ran proof-of-delivery by hand in two depots for the same 186 drivers over eight weeks: six on the original flow, 6 April to 17 May 2026, then two on a rebuilt one, 18 to 31 May. In week six, 41 of 186 completed capture unprompted, or 22.0 per cent; the rebuilt flow cut capture to one barcode scan of about 35 seconds, and in week eight 118 of 186 completed unprompted, or 63.4 per cent. The test cost ₹2.40 lakh, one fifty-ninth of the ₹1.42 crore already committed, and was the first whose measured actor was the driver rather than the owner — the divergence was never fixed, since the owner still signs the cheque; what changed was whose behaviour got measured. Run in March 2025 instead of the letters of intent, thirteen months earlier, it would have stopped the build. As it is, by September 2026 nine of the 14 contractors had committed to renew for the licence year beginning January 2027 at ₹1,80,000 each — ₹16.20 lakh committed, a signed intention and not yet cash.

9. Failure modes, their early warnings and the cost of catching them late

Buying a receipt instead of a signal, from the wrong person. Warning: the word refundable, a deposit "credited against the first invoice", or a usage metric whose commitment came from a budget line. Diagnostic: what does this cost somebody who would not have bought, and is the payer the actor? Late cost: QoFleet's ₹1.42 crore — the signal that authorised the build separated nobody, and the party that gave it was never going to use the thing.

Denominator drift. Warning: stages quoted against different bases, or a base that is the registered rather than the eligible population. Diagnostic: write every stage against one named eligible population, and state the window. Late cost: Quila's first draft read 1.49 per cent and would have killed a business whose tap rate was 7.00 per cent of those who saw the door and whose paid conversion was 0.369 per cent of them.

Treating correlated units as independent, or a cohort as a steady state. Warning: the sample size counts seats, devices or sessions rather than decisions; or a survivor count is set against a threshold defined as a stock. Diagnostic: how many independent entities could have said no, and is the evidence the same kind of quantity as the threshold? Late cost: Lahane would have taken a ₹4.41 crore forecast to a board on evidence that cannot rule out ₹1.10 crore.

Running tests that cannot change the action. Warning: nobody can state the result that would stop the project, often because the request arrived as "something stronger than a survey for Thursday". Diagnostic: write the threshold and both branches before the test. Late cost: the rung-3 fake door above, worth exactly zero against ₹4 lakh — and, repeated, an organisation that keeps the vocabulary of evidence and loses its function.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

One: replace the ladder with likelihood ratios outright. Steelmanned, the decision-analytic case is strong. Rank order only proxies diagnosticity; Quorum's records show a rung-3 test at LR+ 1.03 and a rung-5 test at LR+ 6.40, and the ladder cannot tell a useful test from a useless one of the same height. For it to be wrong, most teams would have to be unable to accumulate four years of paired outcome data — true of the great majority, who have neither 34 resolved assumptions nor a pre-registered bar on record. The heuristic survives because the computation is unavailable, not because it is better.

Two: a randomised free-behaviour test beats an unrandomised paid one. The experimentalist case is that internal validity dominates incentive-compatibility: a randomised test on the shipping surface with thousands of independent users supports a causal claim about the change you will actually make, while a paid pilot of ten volunteers supports nothing causal. Its evidence is the record of A/B tests overturning pilot conclusions. For it to be wrong, free behaviour would have to diverge from the purchase decision in a way randomisation cannot fix — what happens when the free action is a tap and the real one costs ₹1,499.

Three: stated intent is usable at a measured discount. The calibration case is that the ladder throws away cheap information out of squeamishness. Juster-style graded probability questions, calibrated against a firm's own realised conversion, forecast uptake at a fraction of a paid test's cost. For this to be wrong the discount factor would have to be unstable across categories, price points and wordings — which the contingent-valuation literature supports. Both this school and the sacrifice school can be right for different firms: twenty launches of calibration history is a different position from two.

Four: at the organisational seams its function is political, not epistemic. The least comfortable position holds that mature companies rank evidence only until the quarterly plan locks, after which the ladder's value is to give a product manager vocabulary with which to refuse a senior person's conviction. The tell is the direction of the request: "what would change our mind?" is the ladder in use, "something stronger than a survey for Thursday" is rung shopping. The evidence is behavioural: it is cited far more in approval memos than in the design of tests, and stop thresholds are written after the result more often than before. For this to be wrong, adopters would have to show better-calibrated forecasts, not better-argued meetings — a comparison almost nobody runs.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied the ladder names rungs. Someone who has internalised it decomposes a test into assumption-test pairs and gives each its own rung, asks what evidence would be worth before asking what it costs, and will skip a test because no result could change the action. They name the eligible denominator, the count of independent decisions and the difference between a stock and a flow before looking at any rate, and fix the stop threshold in advance. The negative tell is as sharp: a master is unembarrassed about interviews, because they answer questions of mechanism no payment figure can. Lavania's told her households subscribed for a named physician, not the panel — the most expensive line in the cost sheet.

12. Closing: what each of them decided

On 22 September 2026 Lakdawala declined QoVitals as designed, declined structure C, and approved D conditionally: physician review bought per report at ₹240, the dedicated laboratory contract cancelled at ₹95 more per panel, ₹1.20 lakh of fixed cost, break-even 160. She rejected the narrow launch the renewals seemed to recommend, because narrowing cuts subscribers and leaves fixed cost alone — 121 against 160. Two clauses went into the memo: the approval is void if the laboratory renegotiation fails, since with the ₹3.00 lakh minimum break-even is 495 and the launch loses ₹2.75 lakh a quarter; and QoVitals closes if subscribers fall below 160 in two consecutive quarters. She recorded that the ₹8,934 surplus sits inside sampling noise and that the launch rests on an untested flow of new eligible openers, not on proof of demand.

On 9 October 2026 Lahane did not take the ₹4.41 crore number to the board. He wrote the two assumptions down separately, conceded his pilot was rung five for the buying decision and rung three for usage, and conceded that ten accounts cannot distinguish 45 per cent activation from a 35 per cent threshold. He spent ₹11 lakh on a second pilot with randomly selected rather than volunteer accounts, justified by ₹12.38 lakh of decision value against a ₹21 lakh ceiling — while recording that the ₹1.38 lakh of headroom does not survive a weaker test. At LR+ 3.0 with sensitivity held at 0.80 the gain falls to ₹9.40 lakh, below the ₹11 lakh cost; at LR+ 3.0 with specificity held at 0.875 he would build whatever the result said and the test is worth zero. The ₹11 lakh was a judgement call on a borrowed likelihood ratio, not an arithmetic result. He also instrumented the module so customers would configure it themselves.

Three questions for discussion.

1. Lahane's ₹12.38 lakh rests on a likelihood ratio borrowed from a reference class whose success criterion differed from his. At what LR+ does the ₹11 lakh stop paying for itself — and why does the answer depend on whether sensitivity or specificity is the thing that degrades?

2. Lakdawala's launch survives only because a laboratory contract was cancelled. Is that a finding about customer demand at all, and what does it imply about validating demand before designing the cost structure?

3. QoFleet's deposits were real money, signed by real owners, and told Quorum nothing useful. Write the one sentence you would add to your team's experiment template that would have caught it in March 2025.

13. Going deeper

Designing discovery experiments — the cheapest test reaching a chosen rung; it unlocks setting the stop threshold first. Evidence strength: say, do, pay — the same ordering as a sentence you can say in a meeting; the companion page works the Qalam case and reaches the opposite launch verdict, for the reason given in section 6. False positives in discovery — how top-rung evidence still misleads. The four product risks — which assumption to rank first; QoFleet was a viability test run against a usability assumption. Landing-page and smoke tests — the cheapest rung-three instruments, and where denominator discipline is lost. Fake doors and painted doors — Lavania's test, and the ethics of a door onto nothing. Concierge and Wizard of Oz tests — what rescued QoFleet. Pre-sales, LOIs and deposits — top-rung instruments and their refundability traps, read against condition two. Prototype testing — why construct transfer, not fidelity, is the variable that matters.
exp20v2-val.evidence.ladder:
The Evidence Ladder

How strong is my evidence, really: opinion, intent, behaviour, or payment?

1. Opening: a survey that said 47 per cent

On Monday 6 July 2026, Ira Kandhari, head of product at Qalam Learning, a Pune-based subscription app that sells recorded lessons and practice tests to families preparing children for the Class 10 board examinations, opened a slide that her research lead, Ishit Kotwal, had titled "Demand for Qiyas: validated." Qiyas was the working name for a proposed add-on: a live, small-group doubt-clearing session with a human tutor, priced at ₹499 a month. Qalam had 1,20,000 paying households. The slide reported a survey of 400 of them, in which 188 respondents had ticked "definitely" or "probably" when asked whether they would buy Qiyas. That is 188 of 400, or 47 per cent.

Applied to the whole base, 47 per cent meant 56,400 households and, at ₹499, about ₹281 lakh of new revenue every month. The engineering lead, Ilesh Kasbekar, had already estimated the build at two quarters of a two-engineer team, which is twelve engineer-months; at a loaded cost of ₹2.5 lakh per engineer-month (an assumption used throughout this page) that is ₹30 lakh. The finance partner, Ishika Kharpade, had pencilled in tutor costs of ₹1.8 lakh a month, for two full-time tutors, once the service launched. On those figures the decision was easy, and the slide invited the room to make it.

Kandhari did not approve the build. She asked a single question: "Which of these 188 people has ever paid us for something they said they would buy?" Nobody knew. The stakes were concrete: roughly twelve engineer-months and a promise to the board of a new revenue line, against a survey whose answer might say more about politeness than about wallets. This page follows what she did next, because the way she resolved it is the cleanest introduction to a tool product teams call the evidence ladder.

2. The idea

The evidence ladder is a ranking of the kinds of proof you can gather about a customer assumption, ordered by how much it cost the customer to produce that proof. At the bottom sits opinion, which costs the person nothing. At the top sits repeated payment, which costs them real money again and again. The higher the rung, the harder the evidence is to fake, and so the more weight a decision can safely place on it.

The idea was invented to solve a recurring and expensive failure: teams that ask customers what they want, hear yes, build, and then discover that nobody uses the result. Its intellectual lineage is plural. Steve Blank and Eric Ries, writing in the late 2000s, popularised the instruction to test assumptions with cheap experiments before building. Rob Fitzpatrick's The Mom Test (2013) argued that opinions about the future are worthless and that only commitments carry information. Behavioural economists had said much the same for decades, noting that stated and revealed preferences diverge. Studio-style programmes that teach discovery, such as the lab courses at Berkeley SCET, Stanford and Cornell Tech, require teams to test at least one material assumption on a real product, and they grade the strength of the evidence, not the volume of it.

The sentence Kandhari could repeat in a meeting: "Before we ask how many people said yes, let us ask what it cost them to say it."

The ladder does not tell you what to build. It tells you how much confidence a given number deserves, and it prices that confidence in the currency that matters: the customer's own sacrifice.

3. How it actually works

The mechanics have five steps, and practitioners routinely skip the first and the last.

Step one: name the assumption and the rung it is currently on. Kandhari's assumption was not "people like Qiyas." It was "enough households will pay ₹499 a month, and keep paying, to cover a tutor cost of ₹1.8 lakh a month." Written that way, the survey is plainly on rung two. This diagnosis, the explicit placement of existing evidence, is the step most often left implicit.

Step two: decide the rung the decision needs. Evidence required scales with the cost of being wrong. A change to a button colour can rest on rung three. A twelve-engineer-month build with ongoing tutor payroll needs rung five, or at least rung four.

Step three: design the cheapest experiment that reaches that rung. This is the subject of the neighbouring topic on designing discovery experiments. Here, Kasbekar built, in three days, a "fake door": a Qiyas button shown to a random 12,000 of the 1,20,000 households, 10 per cent of the base. Tapping it led to a price page. A further tap on "Reserve" asked for a refundable ₹99 deposit. Households that paid were offered a real month of Qiyas at the full ₹499, run by hand with two part-time tutors. That is far cheaper than the two full-time tutors assumed for the launched service, which is possible only because the pilot cohort was tiny; the ₹1.8 lakh figure below is the cost at scale, not the pilot's cost.

Step four: count at each rung with the same denominator. Every figure below uses the 12,000 households who were shown the button, because that is the population who could have acted. Mixing denominators, for example reporting a payment rate among people who had already clicked next to a click rate among everyone, is the commonest way to flatter a result.

Step five: translate up, and compare with what the decision needs. Convert the observed rate on the highest rung you reached into the quantity the business cares about, here subscribers and rupees, and compare it with the break-even. The result either clears the bar or it does not, and the earlier rungs become useful only as a diagnosis of where interest leaked away.

4. A worked example, line by line

The timeline was as follows. Kasbekar built the fake door on 7 to 9 July. It ran from 13 to 24 July, with deposits taken until 31 July. Month one of the paid pilot ran from 3 August to 2 September, and month two from 3 September to 2 October, about twelve weeks in all after the survey. The numbers below are the ones Kandhari's team reported at the end of that cycle. Table 1 sets out the funnel. Each rate is stated against its own previous stage and also against the 12,000 shown.

Percentages are rounded to the stated places. 540/12,000 = 4.5; 162/540 = 30.0; 61/162 = 37.65; 44/61 = 72.13; 29/44 = 65.91.

Now translate each rung into monthly revenue for the full base of 1,20,000 households, which is ten times the 12,000 sample. Survey: 47 per cent of 1,20,000 is 56,400 households, times ₹499, equals ₹2,81,43,600, or ₹281.44 lakh. Taps: 540 times ten is 5,400 households, times ₹499, equals ₹26,94,600, or ₹26.95 lakh. Deposits: 61 times ten is 610, giving ₹3,04,390, or ₹3.04 lakh. Month-one payers: 440 households, ₹2,19,560, or ₹2.20 lakh. Month-two payers: 290 households, ₹1,44,710, or ₹1.45 lakh.

The ratio is the lesson. The survey promised nearly 195 times what repeated payment delivered. Every step upward shed a large share of the previous rung's apparent demand, and the biggest single-stage loss in households came at the very first step, where 12,000 shown became 540 tapped (11,460 not tapping). Among those who did tap, the largest single-stage loss was 540 to 162 (378 households); the two stages from tap to deposit together took 540 down to 61, a loss of 479.

Next, the decision test. Ishika Kharpade's cost for the full service was ₹1.8 lakh a month, so the break-even subscriber count is 1,80,000 / 499 = 360.7, so 361 households. The observed figure of 290 falls short by 71. The survey-based plan rested on a figure 156 times the break-even (56,400 / 361); the paid evidence says the product loses about ₹35,000 a month (₹1,80,000 minus ₹1,44,710 equals ₹35,290).

Second pass: change one input. Suppose the question is not "build Qiyas for everyone" but "build it for the Class 10 households only." The team had tagged 2,800 of the 12,000 sampled households as having a Class 10 child. Among them, 24 of the 29 month-two payers appeared; the remaining 5 came from the other 9,200 households. Scaled by ten, that is 28,000 Class 10 households yielding 240 subscribers, a rate of 24/2,800 = 0.86 per cent, against 5/9,200 = 0.05 per cent elsewhere. A Class 10-only service needs one tutor, at ₹90,000 a month, so break-even is 90,000 / 499 = 180.4, so 181 subscribers. Revenue of 240 times ₹499 is ₹1,19,760, a margin of ₹29,760 a month. Here margin means monthly revenue less tutor cost only, before any engineering build cost or overhead. On that measure the recommendation changes from "do not run it for everyone" to "run it narrowly," and the sign survives recomputation, but not comfortably. The square root of 24 is about 4.9, so ordinary sampling noise puts the true renewal count somewhere near 19 to 29, which is 190 to 290 subscribers. That range is a one-sigma Poisson range, covering about 68 per cent of outcomes, and is not a confidence interval. The low end clears 181 only narrowly, and if 24 were the true expected count there would be roughly an 11 per cent chance that a cohort of this size produced 18 or fewer renewals, which is below the 18.1 needed for 181 subscribers.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Cost to the customer, not effort for you

Rungs are ordered by what the respondent gives up. A beautifully crafted prototype demo that a customer watches for free is still low on the ladder. A scrappy manual service that someone pays for is high. Do not confuse your own effort with their sacrifice.

A click is behaviour, but weak behaviour

Rung three is real action and therefore better than opinion, yet it costs a few seconds. In the Qalam funnel, 540 households tapped, and only 61 would part with ₹99. Treat a tap as a measure of curiosity about the label on the button.

Small payments test the habit of paying, not the willingness to pay your price

The ₹99 deposit was refundable, so it measured seriousness more than price tolerance. The first full ₹499 payment tests price; the second tests value. That is why month two sits at the top.

The rungs are a gradient, not a switch

Time can be a currency too. A parent who gives forty minutes to an interview, or uploads a child's mark sheet, has paid something. Where the product is free or the buyer is an institution, commitments such as a signed letter of intent, a named pilot owner, or data access stand in for the rupee.

The ladder gauges strength, not truth

Paid usage, 44 households in month one and 29 in month two, says those households value the service; the 61 depositors are rung four, not paid usage. It does not say the other 11,971 households (12,000 less the 29 who renewed) do, and it cannot tell you why the 29 stayed. Strong evidence about a narrow group is still narrow. The next topic in this module, false positives in discovery, deals with how a high rung can still mislead.

Samples are the hidden half of the argument

The Class 10 result rests on 24 renewals. Rate arithmetic carried out to two decimals gives false comfort when the count underneath is small. Always print the count beside the rate.

Lower rungs are not useless

Interviews and surveys are the right tool for generating hypotheses, such as discovering that doubts cluster in physics and mathematics. They are the wrong tool for sizing demand. Use each rung for the question it can answer.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace products; small and large companies

ContextWhat payment looks likeTypical trap
ConsumerA small paid month, a pre-order, a refundable deposit; renewal as the proof.Free-tier clicks mistaken for demand; politeness in surveys.
B2BA paid pilot, a signed letter of intent with a budget line, a named owner, data or integration access.Enthusiastic champions without budget authority; "we love it" from a user who does not buy.
MarketplaceBoth sides, separately: sellers listing real inventory, buyers completing real transactions.Proving one side only; subsidised first transactions that vanish when the subsidy ends.
Early-stageFounder-led sales, hand-delivered service; ten paying customers outweigh a thousand survey replies.Mistaking friendly early adopters for the market.
Large companyInternal budget approval and a transfer price count as commitments; so does a channel partner's purchase order.Surveys commissioned to justify an existing plan; paid evidence resisted because it can say no.

In consumer products, as at Qalam, the rupee is easy to collect and the main challenge is discipline: it is tempting to stop at the tap. In B2B, the rupee is slow, so commitment proxies matter more, and the key question is whether the person speaking holds the budget. In marketplaces, the ladder must be climbed twice, once for supply and once for demand, and a result that holds for one side only is half a result.

The size of the company changes who is allowed to be disappointed. In a start-up, the founder who runs the experiment will usually act on the answer. In a large firm, the people commissioning the evidence frequently have a plan already, and a low-rung result is attractive because it cannot refuse. A discipline that works in large firms is to agree the rung in advance: write down, before the test, what number on which rung would stop the project.

7. Common mistakes

Mistake one: reporting a rung-two number as demand

Symptom: a deck headline of "47 per cent would buy" with no mention of anyone paying. Misunderstanding: treating stated intent as a forecast. Cheapest diagnostic: ask of each statistic, "what did the person give up to produce this?"

Mistake two: switching denominators between rungs

Symptom: a conversion figure that looks excellent, such as 72 per cent, quoted without the 0.37 per cent of the exposed population it describes. Misunderstanding: a stage rate is mistaken for an overall rate. Diagnostic: write the whole funnel against one base, as in Table 1.

Mistake three: stopping at free behaviour

Symptom: the team celebrates 540 taps and schedules the build. Misunderstanding: any behaviour is treated as commitment. Diagnostic: compare the evidence rung with the cost of being wrong, and ask whether a rupee changed hands.

Mistake four: generalising a paid result to a segment that never paid

Symptom: a plan for all 1,20,000 households justified by a result that came almost entirely from Class 10 families. Misunderstanding: an average hides concentration. Diagnostic: split the paid group by the obvious segment variables before extrapolating.

8. What good looks like

Good practice on the same decision would have looked like this. Before the survey, Kandhari's team writes the assumption: "At least 361 households, projected over the whole base, will pay ₹499 for two consecutive months." They agree that the survey can only decide which segments to test, not whether to build. They run the fake door on a random 10 per cent, record every stage against 12,000, and declare three zones in advance. Below 250 projected renewals (about 70 per cent of break-even, a judgement that no segment split is likely to rescue a result that far short) the project stops. At 361 or more it goes ahead. Between 250 and 361 is a declared grey zone with a fixed action: split by segment and test the narrower plan against its own, lower break-even. The observed 290 falls in that zone, so the rule would have produced exactly the action taken, not a surprise. They report each rate beside its count, state the sampling noise, and present the result as "here is what customers paid, and here is what they only said."

HabitQalam, handled well
Assumption and zones written as numbersStop below 250, grey zone 250 to 361, go at 361 or more (full plan, ₹1.8 lakh cost)
Rung stated for each piece of evidenceSurvey on rung 2; funnel on rungs 3 to 5
One denominator12,000 households shown the button
Segment split before extrapolation24 of 29 renewals from 2,800 Class 10 households
Uncertainty printed240 subscribers, plausibly 190 to 290, break-even 181

9. Closing: what Kandhari decided

On Friday 9 October 2026 Ira Kandhari declined the full Qiyas build. The observed 290 renewals sat in the grey zone, below the 361 the full plan needed, so she took the prescribed action and examined the Class 10 segment. There the arithmetic was thin. The monthly margin of ₹29,760 is revenue less tutor cost only, and the twelve-engineer-month build at ₹30 lakh would take 30,00,000 / 29,760, about 101 months or more than eight years, to repay. A narrow build was therefore not justified either. She approved something smaller: run Qiyas for Class 10 households only as a manual service, on existing video-call and payment tools, with one tutor at ₹90,000 a month and no engineering commitment, and review after three months.

She wrote two rules into the approval. Stop: if the first cohort projects below 181 subscribers, Qiyas closes. Build: engineering is considered only if the monthly margin shows a path to repaying ₹30 lakh within 24 months, which means about ₹1.25 lakh a month, far above today's ₹29,760. The survey, she told the board, had been valuable for one thing only: it had pointed her to the question.

To go further, read next on designing discovery experiments, which shows how to construct the cheap test that reaches a given rung, and then on false positives in discovery, which explains how strong-looking evidence can still deceive. The first tells you how to climb; the second tells you what can go wrong at the top.

Two questions to sit with. First, think of the last decision your team made on the strength of a survey, an interview or a stakeholder's confidence: what rung was it, and what would the next rung have cost? Second, if your product is free, or sold to an institution, what is the equivalent of a rupee: what could a customer give up that you would believe?
case20v1-val.evidence.ladder:
Thinnai: What the Pharmacists Said, Did and Paid

A decision case on the evidence ladder

1. Opening

On the morning of Thursday, 15 October 2026, Eswari Lakkaraju sat in a glass meeting room on the second floor of Thinnai's office in Coimbatore with four sets of numbers and one deadline. As head of product, she had to tell the leadership team by Friday, 30 October whether Thinnai should commit ₹180 lakh (₹1.8 crore) to build a refill-reminder product for independent chemists. The board would meet on Friday, 6 November, two days before Diwali, and the investors' next tranche was tied to a clear answer.

The numbers in front of her were all encouraging. Nobody had yet been asked to pay for the product.

2. Company background

Thinnai, named after the raised front porch of a Tamil house where neighbours sit and talk, was founded in 2016 by Ezhilarasan Lakshminarayanan and two classmates. Its core product is billing and inventory software for independent pharmacies, the corner chemists who still dispense most of India's prescription medicines. About 9,000 pharmacies, mostly in Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Telangana and Karnataka, pay an average of ₹900 a month, which gives annual recurring revenue of about ₹9.72 crore (9,000 × ₹900 × 12). In 2025 Thinnai raised a ₹22 crore Series A, released in tranches against milestones.

The market around it is changing. Tata 1mg, PharmEasy and Apollo Pharmacy have taught urban households to expect reminders and home delivery for chronic medicines. A neighbourhood chemist, who knows that Mrs Rao's mother takes a blood-pressure tablet every month, has the relationship but no tool for using it. Thinnai's idea was a module that reads a pharmacy's own billing history and sends a WhatsApp reminder, with the customer's consent under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, a few days before the strip runs out. Payment would be by UPI link. The All India Organisation of Chemists and Druggists (AIOCD) and its state associations gave the idea a warm hearing.

3. The situation

Between August and October, the team gathered evidence in three stages. They did so deliberately, but nobody had written down beforehand what each stage was meant to prove.

The first was a survey. Between 3 and 14 August, Thinnai invited 240 chemists through association WhatsApp groups. Of these, 150 responded, and 111 of the 150 said they would probably or definitely pay ₹1,500 a month for the module. The second was a landing page, live from 17 August to 13 September, which drew 3,200 visits from distinct pharmacies. A total of 192 joined the waitlist and 48 of those booked a demo call. The third was a free pilot from 14 September to 11 October with 30 pharmacies in Coimbatore, Madurai and Hyderabad. Exhibit 1 sets these out, and Exhibit 2 shows the timeline.

The global team read the numbers differently. Ethiraj Loganathan, who leads engineering from Pune, wanted to start building at once: his six engineers could finish a first release by April, and the Hyderabad pilot pharmacies were already asking for the module to be kept on after the pilot. Elena Lingaiah, the data scientist in Toronto, had analysed the pilot logs and warned that every figure in them came from pharmacies that had volunteered. Eugene Lakshmipathy, the customer-success lead in Singapore, who had called most of the pilot pharmacists, reported something quieter: several liked the product but said "let us see" when the price came up.

4. The people

Ezhilarasan Lakshminarayanan, chief executive in Coimbatore, wants an answer before the board meets. Ethiraj Loganathan, in Pune, wants the build to begin now; a team kept waiting loses momentum, and two of his senior engineers have outside offers. Elena Lingaiah, in Toronto, wants the company to separate what the logs show from what they cannot show. Eugene Lakshmipathy, in Singapore, wants to protect pharmacist relationships and does not want customers to feel that a free pilot has turned into a sales trap.

5. The pilot in detail

Exhibit 3 gives the pilot results by city. Of the 30 pharmacies, 21 were active. Across all 30, 18,900 reminders were sent, and 2,646 refills were bought within seven days of a reminder, a rate of 14.0 per cent of reminders sent.

Eswari knew what this table could not say. A customer who received a reminder might have refilled that week anyway, since the pilot had no comparison group of customers who were not reminded. The 14.0 per cent was therefore a measure of use, not of lift. Used this way, the pilot reached the behaviour rung of the ladder: people did something with the product on their own time. It did not reach the payment rung.

The economics make the gap matter. At the quoted price of ₹1,500 a month, a pharmacy pays ₹18,000 a year. To earn ₹180 lakh in revenue, before any running cost, Thinnai would need 1,000 pharmacy-years, for instance 500 paying pharmacies for two years. That is 5.6 per cent of the 9,000-pharmacy base (500 ÷ 9,000). No evidence collected so far shows that one chemist will actually part with ₹1,500.

6. The options

Option A: build now. Commit the ₹180 lakh over six months, using the survey, waitlist and pilot as justification. The upside is speed: a release by April 2027 and a team kept together. The cost is that the whole sum rests on the first three rungs, and poor conversion would surface only after launch.

Option B: run a paid test first. Between 2 November and 4 December, ask the 21 active pilot pharmacies to prepay ₹6,000 by UPI for four months of the service, with no promise of refund beyond a service failure. The cost is about ₹6 lakh in onboarding and visits, plus a delay of roughly five weeks. The upside is the only evidence that includes a rupee. The limit is that the 21 are friendly volunteers, so a result would be a ceiling on what the wider base might do, not an estimate of it.

Option C: widen the survey. Spend about ₹3 lakh on a survey of 1,000 more chemists across four states, taking about three weeks. This would give a larger and more varied sample, and it would be cheap. It would also leave Thinnai on the opinion rung, with a more precise version of the same answer.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. For each row of Exhibit 1, state what the person did, and what they would have had to do to move up one rung. Which rung has Thinnai actually reached?
  2. The survey shows 74.0 per cent and the pilot 70.0 per cent. Why are these two figures not evidence of the same thing, and why does the 46.25 per cent of invited chemists matter?
  3. What does Exhibit 3 show, and what can it not show? What would Elena need in order to claim that reminders cause refills?
  4. Choose between the three options. What result in the chosen test would change your mind, and what would you decide before the test begins?

8. A note for the learner

The evidence ladder ranks what people tell you by how much it cost them to tell you. Opinion costs a sentence. Intent costs a few minutes. Behaviour costs time and habit. Payment costs money, and money is the rung at which a customer is deciding about a real alternative use of that money. Each experiment buys one rung, and a case such as this is mostly about noticing that all of Thinnai's evidence sits below the top.

A well-reasoned answer begins by naming the rung, then asks which unproven assumption would sink the investment if wrong. Here that assumption is willingness to pay, since the module's technical feasibility has been shown. Option C is weakest because it adds more of the evidence Thinnai already has. Option A is not foolish; it fits if the cost of waiting exceeds the cost of being wrong, but Ethiraj's concern about momentum can be met in other ways, and ₹6 lakh is 3.3 per cent of the ₹180 lakh it protects.

One defensible path is Option B with the rule written down now. If at least 11 of the 21 pharmacies pay (just over half), release the first tranche of the build. If between 6 and 10 pay, build nothing yet and test a lower price or a shorter commitment. These cut-offs are judgement calls, not computed values. If 5 or fewer pay, stop. Meanwhile Ethiraj's team works on the core billing roadmap, so the five weeks cost time to market, not idle salaries. Eugene should lead the ask, because the pharmacists already trust him. Elena should also run a small holdout, in which some customers are not reminded, so that the next review can speak about lift and not only use.

A pass would show that friendly, active pharmacists will pay; it would not prove that 500 more will. That is why the path funds a first tranche rather than the entire sum.

Indian School of Business · Discovery & Assumption Testing

Vinimaya Technologies: What Does the Evidence Buy?

Five studies and ₹86.20 lakh sit behind a module a Bengaluru product leader must launch in four weeks. On Sunday night she is working out what any of it proves.

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on the night of Sunday, 11 October 2026, Gopika Muthukrishnan sat on the floor of her flat in Indiranagar with eleven printed slides fanned out around her. In ten hours the board of Vinimaya Technologies Private Limited would take up one item: ₹28.00 crore over eighteen months to launch Vinimaya Pulse, the demand-forecast module, as a paid subscription at ₹1,499 per outlet per month across the distributor network the company had spent four years building.

Muthukrishnan, vice-president of product, had owned Pulse since the first scoping note and was not opposed to the launch. What had kept her awake since Thursday was that, of the company's five studies, she could no longer say which had told her anything she did not already believe.

On top was her own slide, built fourteen months earlier for an investor update: 76% of retailers say they want demand forecasting. Below it, the chief financial officer's slide of Tuesday, 29 September, turning a tap on a notification card into ₹98.97 crore of annual revenue (Exhibit 2). At the bottom lay the June device audit, which had taken apart the study everyone still called proof that shopkeepers would pay. Pulse was either a ₹99 crore business or a feature nine shopkeepers had bought with their own money, and the paper on her floor fitted both.

2. The company, and a signature from 2022

Vinimaya was founded in Bengaluru in 2018 by Ganapathy Malladi and Gunaseelan Moorthy, who had met selling software to consumer goods distributors in the Deccan belt. Its first product, shipped in March 2019, was Vinimaya Ledger: GST-compliant invoicing, e-way bills and credit notes for distributors being pushed onto electronic invoicing. In the year ended 31 March 2026 that business still produced ₹37.40 crore of the company's ₹46.80 crore of revenue.

The decision that shaped everything after it was signed on 1 July 2022. To become the sole retailer-facing platform for Vakula Trade Networks Private Limited, a Hyderabad super-distributor with routes across Telangana, Andhra Pradesh and north Karnataka, Vinimaya accepted a five-year agreement to 30 June 2027. Vakula pays ₹41 per contracted outlet per month — ₹80.57 lakh a month, ₹9.67 crore a year on the 1,96,500 outlets contracted at 30 September 2026 — and Vinimaya agreed not to sell directly outside the network for the life of the agreement.

The clause bought scale no competitor could match, but it also means every retailer Vinimaya has observed was recruited, trained, surveyed and supported by an organisation whose own incentive is to keep kirana shelves loyal to Vakula's brands. The company has never sold anything to a shopkeeper not standing in front of a field officer.

3. The industry

India's general trade still moves most packaged goods through roughly thirteen million small outlets, and every large player wants the software layer on the shopkeeper's phone. Reliance Retail pushes JioMart Partner; Udaan, ElasticRun and Jumbotail run ordering apps; Khatabook took the ledger; quick commerce — Zepto, Blinkit, Swiggy Instamart — is pulling the impulse basket out of the kirana store in the metros where Vakula earns best.

Payments are no longer a moat: UPI is free rails, and the ₹1 pre-authorisation Vinimaya used as a commitment test was possible only because NPCI's plumbing makes a one-rupee mandate trivial. Regulation now bites hardest on data. With the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules notified last November, Vinimaya's lawyers hold that the company processes outlet data as Vakula's processor under the 2022 agreement, and that selling directly to the same outlet would make it a fiduciary in its own right, needing its own notice and consent for the eighteen months of history the automated forecast requires.

Exposure is not only domestic: the demonstration has produced letters of intent from Verdant Gulf Trading LLC in Dubai and Vermilion Supply Partners in New Jersey (Exhibit 5). Engineering sits in Bengaluru and Pune, data science in Toronto, design in Berlin, customer success in Singapore and sales in New Jersey, so those who most doubt the Indian evidence sit furthest from the shops.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Pulse began as a request from Vakula's sales planners in early 2025: give the shopkeeper a weekly suggested order and the beat plan becomes self-fulfilling. Between June 2025 and April 2026 the company ran five studies, each treated inside Vinimaya as confirming the last; Exhibit 1 gives their bases and Exhibit 6 their cost.

The June 2025 survey was run by telephone by Vakula's field officers. Of 2,140 outlets dialled, 1,286 completed the module-interest section, and 974 of those said they would definitely subscribe — 75.7 per cent, which became "76% of retailers" on the investor slide. Nobody then recorded the officers' adoption incentive, or that the 854 non-completions were dropped rather than counted as negatives.

In August 2025 the team shipped a notification card inside the app, shown only to outlets that had opened it in each of the four preceding weeks: 18,400 of them. There were 5,152 taps on "Notify me", exactly 28.0 per cent of those shown the card — the planning number ever since, including in a model applying it to all 1,96,500 contracted outlets.

September 2025 brought what everyone agreed was the real test. In Hubballi and Vijayawada, 1,236 waitlisted outlets were shown a screen asking for a ₹1 UPI pre-authorisation to hold an early-access slot; 389 completed it, 31.5 per cent, and a commitment rate above the tap rate was read as intent hardening as the ask got costlier. In June 2026 Gokul Mahalingam audited the devices behind those mandates: 212 had been completed on 23 handsets, each carrying a field officer's login. From the outlets' own devices there were 177 mandates, 14.3 per cent of the 1,236.

The concierge pilot ran fourteen weeks, from Monday 6 October 2025 to Sunday 11 January 2026, across 412 outlets field officers picked from the 1,236. Each weekly forecast was part model, part two Pune analysts at about an hour per outlet a month — a fact absent from the pilot summary. Usage fell as Exhibit 3 shows, from 340 outlets in week 1 to 148 in week 14. Over the final eight weeks the forecast came within ten per cent of recorded offtake in 1,642 of 3,296 outlet-weeks (49.8 per cent), against 1,121 for the outlet's own standing order (34.0 per cent) — but that offtake is Vakula's dispatch record, itself a partial response to the forecast.

Then the priced offer, 9 February to 23 April 2026: 96 outlets, drawn from the 148 still weekly-active in week 14, were offered Pulse at ₹1,499 a month. Thirty-one subscribed, 32.3 per cent. Twenty-two had the fee rebated against their trade margin by Vakula, leaving 9 paying from their own accounts — 9.4 per cent of the 96. At 31 August 2026, 19 of the 31 were still paying (61.3 per cent): 15 of the 22 rebated outlets (68.2 per cent) and 4 of the 9 unsubsidised ones (44.4 per cent).

8. The options as Muthukrishnan sees them

She had written four on the back of the Exhibit 2 printout. One: launch at ₹1,499 before Diwali, take Vakula's ₹6.80 crore of onboarding, and accept that the first honest read on willingness to pay arrives in March 2027, the ₹28.00 crore already committed. Two: hold ninety days and run a randomised price ladder — ₹499, ₹999 and ₹1,499 against a holdout — in two districts with Vinimaya's own staff, letting Vakula's offer lapse. Three: build the white-label first, where a counterparty signs. Four: stop charging retailers, fold Pulse into the platform fee, and enter the June 2027 renewal asking Vakula for ₹85 an outlet instead of ₹41.

Written out, each assumed something untested. All four take Pulse to be a forecasting product, when the one action Exhibit 4 ties to the forecast in the logs is an order line changed within 48 hours, by 97 of the 412 — an ordering-timing product, which might belong to Vakula's planners. All four assume the customer is the outlet, when the only party that has ever paid Vinimaya at scale is a distributor; all four treat ₹28.00 crore as one decision, though the board's template allows a staged release; and all four ask when to launch — Malladi's question from September — not what she would need to see to believe the module is worth ₹1,499 to a shopkeeper who is not looking at a field officer.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at 9:30 on Monday, 12 October 2026, and the ₹28.00 crore is a single approval: ₹9.60 crore of engineering, ₹11.40 crore of field onboarding, ₹3.20 crore of data infrastructure, ₹2.40 crore of marketing and ₹1.40 crore of contingency. Five seats: Malladi, Moorthy, two nominees of Vikasa Growth Capital, which led the ₹168 crore Series B in March 2024, and Godavari Mandava, an independent director from Chennai consumer goods, who has twice asked for "the paid cohort, not the pilot" and has not been sent Exhibit 1.

Cash at 30 September 2026 was ₹94.60 crore against net burn of ₹4.20 crore a month from 1 October 2026 — 22.5 months of runway, to about mid-August 2028. Spending ₹28.00 crore gross over eighteen months adds ₹1.56 crore a month, taking burn to ₹5.76 crore and runway to 16.4 months, about mid-February 2028; the 30 June 2027 renewal falls nine months in, with ₹42.76 crore left. Vakula's co-funding letter of 2 October 2026 lapses on 24 October and is conditional on go-live before Diwali. The 2022 exclusivity bars any retailer-facing sale outside the network until 30 June 2027, so no independent sample of Indian shopkeepers is lawfully available before then. Munagala needs twelve to fourteen weeks for the automated forecast; Ganesh Meenakshisundaram's 22-person customer-success team in Singapore hand-held 412 outlets in the pilot; headcount is frozen at 54 engineers.
